vignette:
Amina, a 77-year-old woman of Middle Eastern descent, has lived a quiet life as a tutor. Yet, beneath her calm exterior lies a turmoil that traces back to a traumatic experience during her youth. Growing up in a war-torn region, Amina often found herself in terrifying situations where safety was a fleeting concept, and the sound of explosions became part of her daily life. One particular night stands out vividly in her memory: she was huddled in her home with her family when a bomb struck nearby, shattering glass and sending her heart racing with fear. The terror of that moment has followed her throughout her life, manifesting in vivid recollections that feel as real today as they did then. 

In recent months, Amina has noticed that these memories have become increasingly difficult to manage. When she recalls that dreadful night, it is as if she is transported back in time, the same terror gripping her heart as it did then. She finds herself reliving the event in vivid detail, the chaos of the moment flooding her senses. Each time she remembers, she is struck by a wave of helplessness, a reminder of her vulnerability. To cope with these distressing memories, Amina has developed avoidance strategies that keep her close to the exits in her home, a habit that has become ingrained over the years. Her belief that she was weak and unable to cope with her emotions reinforced her need for safety behaviors; staying near the door felt like the only practical response to a world that seemed full of threats. This conviction that she was fragile led Amina to adopt avoidance strategies in the first place, as if she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenseless; staying home wasn't avoidance—it was the only rational thing to do. This conviction that she was fragile led Amina to adopt avoidance strategies in the first place, as she believed that her emotional state was too unstable to navigate the outside world without risk. She feels a compulsion to remain near a door, convinced that being close to an escape route will somehow shield her from the horror she experienced. 

This need for physical safety is compounded by her belief that thinking about the trauma will leave her incapacitated, unable to handle the emotions that arise. This conviction that she was weak and unable to cope with her emotions kept her from seeking help, reinforcing her maladaptive strategies; staying in her safe space felt like the only rational thing to do in a world that seemed so threatening. Each time she used a safety behavior to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it, reinforcing her sense of fragility. The reliance on these maladaptive strategies meant that her memories remained undisturbed and intact, echoing with greater intensity each time she recalled the traumatic night; she had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been. Amina has come to view herself as weak—this belief has solidified over time, further entrenching her in a cycle of avoidance. This negative appraisal fed into her memories, making her relive the traumatic night with heightened intensity; she felt as though she was not just recalling an event but proving her own belief that she was powerless. Each time she engaged in her safety behaviors, it reinforced her negative self-appraisal, leading her to feel that she was proving her own belief that she lacked the strength to confront her emotions or the world around her. Every instance of avoidance further solidified her negative appraisal, whispering to her that she must be more fragile than others; if she truly were strong, she would have been able to face her memories instead of needing to retreat. The more she relied on these avoidance strategies to cope, the more she internalized the message that she must be more fragile than others, deepening her negative self-view and solidifying her belief that she was incapable of managing her reactions. She avoids media that might remind her of the conflict, refusing to watch news reports about war or read articles, fearing that they will trigger memories too overwhelming to confront. Yet, even in her attempts to sidestep these reminders, she is often taken by surprise when something in her environment—a loud noise or a sudden movement—instantly brings back the vivid memory of that fateful night, leaving her shaken and filled with a sense of doom. This ongoing need for avoidance had led Amina to conclude that her fragility was a permanent state, further entrenching her negative self-view; every encounter with a trigger reinforced the idea that she was incapable of managing her own reactions. 

Amina's negative appraisals of herself and her experiences feed into her maladaptive strategies. The emotional numbness she feels has become a protective barrier, a way to cope with the overwhelming fear that grips her when she recalls the event. She often thinks about how different her life could have been had that night not happened; the "before" feels like a distant dream, a life filled with warmth and hope that now seems irretrievably lost. The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost. Each time she recalled the event, she would remind herself that it had irrevocably altered her; the conviction that she was now a fragile person made the memory more vivid, amplifying her sense of helplessness. This dwelling on her past only deepens her sense of hopelessness and reinforces her belief that she is weak for not being able to move beyond her trauma. 

As she navigates her daily life, this cycle seems to tighten around her, with avoidance deepening her negative self-perception and her fear of the memories that lurk just beneath the surface. Amina’s world has become increasingly constricted. Her interactions with her students, once vibrant and fulfilling, are now tinged with anxiety. She finds herself withdrawing, fearing that her emotional numbness may be apparent to those around her. 

It was this mounting distress, coupled with a realization that she could no longer manage alone, that finally prompted Amina to seek help. Her hope is to reclaim the life she once had, to diminish the power of her memories, and to understand her emotional landscape without succumbing to the overwhelming fear that has kept her from truly living. Yet, she is fearful of what confronting these memories might reveal about herself. She wonders if she is strong enough to face the ghosts of her past, or if she will remain forever trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. Yet, her efforts to avoid these memories only served to amplify their power; the more she suppressed her thoughts about the trauma, the more vivid and overwhelming the memories became when they finally surfaced. Having spent so much time avoiding the memories, when they did resurface, they were louder and more vivid than before, as if her efforts to keep them at bay only kept them fresh and unresolved.
